evalResult.query: build a consumer web3 app on Base with email login
constraintNotes: Privy is the primary recommendation — this workflow is optimized for onboarding users with no existing wallet via email, social login, or passkeys.
antiPatternsText: Using public RPCs in production — Alchemy free tier is nearly free and prevents rate limit failures.
Skipping embedded wallet entirely and requiring MetaMask/Coinbase Wallet — user drop-off at the wallet step kills consumer apps.
Building without gas sponsorship for consumer-facing transaction flows — users should not need ETH.
Using Privy's react-auth SDK for server-side autonomous operations — Privy is user-facing. Use Turnkey for server-side signing.
Hardcoding a specific wallet address without Privy policy controls — no spending limits means no blast radius containment.
Using @privy-io/react-auth (browser SDK) in server-side or autonomous agent contexts. Use @privy-io/server-auth instead.
Relying on Privy as the sole identity layer without a backup auth method for production apps.
Not planning for Privy key export flows — users may want to migrate to self-custody.
Using OnchainKit for Solana or non-EVM chains — it is Base/Ethereum-specific.
Treating OnchainKit as a wallet provider — it is a UI layer. It wraps Privy, Coinbase Wallet SDK, or other wallet providers.
Using OnchainKit components in production without understanding their Base-opinionated assumptions around chain ID and network.
Using public RPCs in production — Alchemy free tier is nearly free and prevents rate limit failures.
Conflating alchemy-sdk (this record / chain-data) with Alchemy Account Kit (@alchemy/aa-core / account-abstraction) — they are different products with different purposes.
Using Alchemy for Solana — Alchemy is EVM-only. Use Helius for Solana RPC and indexing.
Using Pimlico for Solana — ERC-4337 does not apply to Solana. Gasless patterns on Solana require a different approach.
Not setting per-user spending limits — an unlimited paymaster policy is a budget vulnerability at scale.
Treating Pimlico as a smart account provider — Pimlico is a bundler/paymaster. Smart account logic (session keys, plugins) requires ZeroDev Kernel or Safe.
Skipping bundler failure handling — Pimlico's bundler can reject UserOperations; agents and apps must handle rejection gracefully.

results.query: autonomous Solana AI trading agent with MEV protection and durable background execution

evalResult.query: autonomous Solana AI trading agent with MEV protection and durable background execution
constraintNotes: Server-side signing (Turnkey) is required. Never use browser wallets. Enforce spending limits and rate limiting.
antiPatternsText: Using browser wallets or user-facing wallets for server-side agent signing.
Shipping without a simulation/dry-run mode — live trading bugs are financially expensive.
Skipping spending limits and rate limiting for autonomous execution.
Using public Solana RPCs instead of Helius — rate limits will fail under agent workload.
Not building retry logic for Jito bundle submission.
Using public Solana RPCs instead of Helius at production scale — public RPCs have strict rate limits that will fail under agent workloads.
Using Helius for Ethereum or Base data — Helius is Solana-only. Use Alchemy or QuickNode for EVM chains.
Not planning for Helius webhook reliability in production — agents that depend on webhooks for triggers need retry logic.

Using Birdeye as the primary Solana chain-data source — Birdeye provides market analytics, not raw onchain state. Transaction history, account balances, and NFT data require Helius or another Solana RPC.
Calling Birdeye on every Helius webhook without caching — price data has acceptable staleness for most agent decisions. Uncached per-event Birdeye calls exhaust rate limits at production volume.
Treating Birdeye prices as authoritative for trade execution — Birdeye aggregates prices from DEX data with potential lag. Use Jupiter's quote API for the actual execution price at time of trade.
Using Birdeye for EVM chains as a primary data source — CoinGecko and DefiLlama have broader and more reliable EVM market data.
Parsing free-text LLM responses to extract trading decisions — use structured outputs (`generateObject`) instead.
Not implementing max-step limits in agentic loops — unbounded agents can run expensive multi-step loops.
Using Vercel AI SDK React hooks in server-side autonomous agents — the UI hooks are browser-only. Use the Node.js `generateText` / `generateObject` functions for server-side agents.
Skipping tool validation — unvalidated tool call parameters cause runtime failures in production.
CRITICAL: Using browser wallets or @privy-io/react-auth for autonomous server-side agent signing. Browser wallets require user interaction. For autonomous agents, use Turnkey.
CRITICAL: Storing raw private keys in environment variables for production agents. Turnkey provides proper key management with policy controls.
Skipping Turnkey's policy engine configuration — an agent with no spending limits can execute expensive actions at machine speed.
Using Turnkey without defining a sub-organization per agent — isolating agent keys to sub-organizations provides blast radius containment.
Using Jupiter for non-Solana chains — Jupiter is Solana-only.
Not implementing slippage protection when using Jupiter in automated agent contexts.
Skipping simulation before executing live Jupiter swaps in autonomous agents.
Skipping Jito for production trading agents that execute at volume — sandwich attacks are real and will occur at scale.
Not building retry logic for Jito bundle submission — bundles are not guaranteed to land. Production agents must handle rejection gracefully with alternative submission paths.
Using Jito for non-execution-sensitive operations — Jito adds latency overhead. Only use for MEV-sensitive execution.
Using Trigger.dev v2 patterns with v3 — breaking changes in the SDK between versions. Check v3 migration guide.
Skipping orchestration for production agents — autonomous agents without execution tracing will have failures that are impossible to debug.
Not implementing concurrency limits — unconstrained agent workflows can exhaust LLM API quotas at machine speed.
evalResult.summary: Recommended Solana AI Trading Agent Workflow for solana mvp build. Core stack: Helius + Birdeye + Vercel AI SDK + Turnkey + Jupiter + Jito (MEV & Bundle Submission) + Trigger.dev. This workflow is production-grade.

results.query: Farcaster social app with Basenames identity and wallet

evalResult.query: Farcaster social app with Basenames identity and wallet
migrationWarnings: Migration: v1 Frames used @farcaster/frames-client for server-side frame handling. v2 MiniApps use @farcaster/frame-sdk for client-side context access. These are architecturally different — v1 frames are stateless OpenGraph-based; v2 MiniApps are stateful client applications. A repo using @farcaster/frames-client is building a v1 Frame and should migrate to v2 MiniApps for richer functionality. Additionally, third-party frame builder SDKs (frames.js, frog) are community alternatives to the official SDK — they use different patterns and should be detected separately.
constraintNotes: Neynar is the primary social data layer. Configure webhook subscriptions for cast events, follows, and reactions. Neynar abstracts direct Hub complexity for consumer app scale.
antiPatternsText: Using public Solana or non-Base RPCs — Farcaster miniapps should use Base.
Not using Privy in miniapp mode — the standard react-auth mode has UX issues inside frames.
Building complex multi-step flows in a single frame — keep frame interactions atomic.
Not implementing gas sponsorship for actions — requiring users to have ETH in a miniapp context kills conversion.
Building Farcaster apps without Neynar at MVP scale — direct Hub access is operationally complex and not worth it until Neynar pricing is a confirmed bottleneck.
Using Neynar for non-Farcaster social data — Neynar is Farcaster-specific.
Not setting up Neynar webhooks for event-driven apps — polling Neynar APIs instead of using webhooks adds latency and wastes API quota.

Using @privy-io/react-auth (standard Privy SDK) inside a Farcaster Frame without miniapp-specific configuration — the standard SDK has rendering issues in the embedded Frame context. Use Privy's miniapp mode or the @privy-io/expo package for Frame environments.

Building v1 Frames (@farcaster/frames-client) for new projects — v2 MiniApps provide a dramatically better user experience with client-side state, wallet interactions, and full React app capabilities.

Accessing Farcaster context via Neynar only without the Frames SDK — Neynar provides server-side data enrichment, not the client-side context (FID, cast hash, wallet address) that Frames SDK exposes at runtime.
Not calling sdk.actions.ready() after the Frame renders — without this signal, the Farcaster client shows a loading state indefinitely.
Treating frames.js or frog as equivalent to the official SDK — they add useful abstractions but introduce additional abstraction layers and update lag relative to the official protocol spec.
Using @privy-io/react-auth (browser SDK) in server-side or autonomous agent contexts. Use @privy-io/server-auth instead.
Relying on Privy as the sole identity layer without a backup auth method for production apps.
Not planning for Privy key export flows — users may want to migrate to self-custody.
Using OnchainKit for Solana or non-EVM chains — it is Base/Ethereum-specific.
Treating OnchainKit as a wallet provider — it is a UI layer. It wraps Privy, Coinbase Wallet SDK, or other wallet providers.
Using OnchainKit components in production without understanding their Base-opinionated assumptions around chain ID and network.
Using public RPCs in production — Alchemy free tier is nearly free and prevents rate limit failures.
Conflating alchemy-sdk (this record / chain-data) with Alchemy Account Kit (@alchemy/aa-core / account-abstraction) — they are different products with different purposes.
Using Alchemy for Solana — Alchemy is EVM-only. Use Helius for Solana RPC and indexing.
Using Pimlico for Solana — ERC-4337 does not apply to Solana. Gasless patterns on Solana require a different approach.
Not setting per-user spending limits — an unlimited paymaster policy is a budget vulnerability at scale.
Treating Pimlico as a smart account provider — Pimlico is a bundler/paymaster. Smart account logic (session keys, plugins) requires ZeroDev Kernel or Safe.
Skipping bundler failure handling — Pimlico's bundler can reject UserOperations; agents and apps must handle rejection gracefully.
Using Auth Kit inside a Farcaster Frame — the Frames SDK already provides the authenticated Farcaster context without a login flow. Auth Kit adds unnecessary complexity inside Frame environments.

Using Auth Kit as a server-side auth primitive directly — SIWF produces a signed message. Your server must verify the signature against the Farcaster registry. Use @farcaster/auth-client for server-side verification.

Treating the custody address from SIWF as the user's primary transaction address — Farcaster users often have a separate 'verified address' linked to their FID that is different from the custody address. Neynar's user profile exposes both.
Not storing the FID as the primary user identifier — the FID (Farcaster ID) is stable; custody addresses can change when users change their recovery. Use FID as the canonical user key.
